regional_overview: The dominant regional story this week is a structural inversion: the countries conducting the most intensive combat operations — UAE (dozens of airstrikes on Iran, including a joint strike on Asaluyeh for which Netanyahu publicly claimed sole Israeli responsibility to protect UAE deniability) and Saudi Arabia (MBS's first on-the-record combat acknowledgment at the Mina Palace Eid reception, MoD casualties confirmed through Hajj logistics notices) — are simultaneously the countries most architecturally excluded from the four multilateral tracks defining the post-war order. Into this vacuum, Turkey's Foreign Minister Fidan used a Nikkei Asia interview to propose a regional security platform naming Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Gulf states — precisely the excluded actors — while Pakistan was formally designated Washington's "primary interlocutor" for Iran-US talks and confirmed to have deployed a jet squadron and thousands of troops to Saudi Arabia under the SMDA. India, hosting the 11th Quad FM Meeting in New Delhi with explicit UNCLOS/Hormuz reaffirmation language, and conducting a bilateral with Saudi FM Faisal bin Farhan at the EU Gymnich in Cyprus, is building institutional architecture around the chokepoint both countries depend on. The Iran peace deal, described as "largely negotiated" as of May 24, did not close: Iran's Ghalibaf and Araghchi both explicitly dismissed deal prospects by May 31, extending the strategic limbo that every country in this region is navigating simultaneously.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Combat-Diplomacy Inversion: Gulf's Most Active Military Participants Structurally Excluded from Post-War Architecture
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: The countries conducting the most intensive offensive military operations — UAE (dozens of airstrikes on Iran, including a joint strike on Asaluyeh with Israeli deniability cover) and Saudi Arabia (first combat acknowledgment via Eid reception remarks; MoD casualties documented through Hajj logistics) — are simultaneously excluded from all four multilateral tracks defining the post-war regional order: the nuclear deal negotiations, Hormuz governance, the Lebanon clause, and the Abraham Accords framework. Into this structural vacancy, Turkey's Fidan proposed a Turkey-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia-Egypt-Gulf security platform in his Nikkei Asia interview, and Pakistan was formally designated by Rubio as Washington's 'primary interlocutor' for Iran-US talks. Both Turkey and Pakistan are gaining structural diplomatic positioning while doing less of the direct military fighting — Turkey through its NATO hosting role and bilateral access to both Washington and Tehran, Pakistan through Munir's two Tehran visits in a single week and SMDA military presence in Saudi Arabia. The inversion is sharpest for Saudi Arabia: it is funding the war through a deficit trajectory (76% of annual target consumed in Q1), fighting an undeclared war, and watching Turkey name it as a potential platform member rather than being an architect of the mechanisms that will determine the post-war order.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: This inversion — where military contribution and diplomatic positioning are inversely correlated — creates structural instability in any post-war settlement. Saudi Arabia and UAE cannot be seen domestically as having paid in blood and fiscal capacity for an order they had no hand in designing. Turkey's platform proposal is analytically significant precisely because it offers a vehicle through which the excluded actors could gain institutional presence — but it is Turkey's initiative, not Saudi Arabia's or UAE's, and its realization depends on Erdoğan's pre-NATO positioning with Trump succeeding.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: PK has no formal desk entry this week; Pakistan's role is sourced through SA and TR desk references to Pakistani deployments and the PK posture note, not a confidence-scored weekly entry. The dynamic does not depend on PK's own assessment — it holds on SA, AE, and TR alone — but the Pakistan elevation dimension carries the posture note's implicit lower confidence.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: The 'exclusion' framing for Saudi Arabia rests primarily on a houseofsaud.com analysis (Tier 3) characterizing the MBS-Iran call as 'the only channel available' — the desk itself flags this as a competing framing that updates the 'expanding leverage' assessment. Saudi Arabia may have more informal multilateral influence than the formal track exclusion suggests; FM Faisal's Gymnich participation documents an ability to insert into European crisis management formats that the 'excluded' label understates. Additionally, Fidan's platform proposal is a single interview signal from a foreign minister whose domestic principal is managing an early-election crisis — it may be diplomatic positioning for the Erdoğan-Trump bilateral rather than a genuine institutional initiative with Saudi buy-in.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The connection is structural, not merely temporal: houseofsaud.com's identification of the four multilateral tracks from which Saudi Arabia is excluded is analytically grounded and directly paralleled by UAE's deniability requirement preventing it from claiming credit for its own strikes. Fidan's platform proposal naming these specific excluded actors — Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Gulf states — in the same week that Saudi Arabia's exclusion is being documented by specialist analysis is more than coincidence. The mechanism is the gap itself: the platform is being proposed because the gap exists. The causal arrow runs from exclusion to proposal.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: Turkey may be proposing the regional platform not to compensate for Saudi exclusion but to create a multilateral vehicle that enhances Turkey's own broker status and gives Erdoğan a pre-NATO deliverable for the Trump bilateral. The named members (Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Egypt, Gulf states) may be selected for their legitimacy-lending function rather than because Turkey has assessed their actual desire to participate. Saudi Arabia may be content with its bilateral channels — MBS-Pezeshkian and MBS-Trump — without needing a new institutional format.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Gulf Parallel Deniability Architecture: SA and AE Calibrate Combat Acknowledgment Through Non-Military Channels Simultaneously
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: Saudi Arabia and UAE have independently converged on structurally identical deniability architectures for acknowledging an undeclared war. Saudi Arabia acknowledged combat through two non-military channels simultaneously: MBS's ceremonial Eid reception remarks to military commanders and the Grand Mufti, and a Hajj logistics notice allocating camps for 'martyrs and injured personnel' under Khalid bin Salman's authority. UAE maintained deniability for its dozens of airstrikes — including the Asaluyeh joint strike with Israel — by accepting Netanyahu's public claim of sole Israeli responsibility as cover. Both architectures accomplish the same function: military families and domestic audiences receive acknowledgment of sacrifice through religious ritual and operational logistics; the war remains without official name, operational designation, or casus belli under domestic law; and no formal declaration that would trigger international legal obligations or create a documented casus belli for escalatory Iranian retaliation. MBZ expressed frustration to MBS when Gulf neighbors refused to coordinate military responses — a detail from the AE desk that confirms SA-AE bilateral security dialogue is occurring even as it is absent from formal diplomatic channels.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: The parallel deniability architecture is not merely a communications strategy — it is the structural condition that makes continued offensive operations politically sustainable in both countries. If either state breaks deniability formally, it creates pressure on the other's domestic political management. The architecture is mutually reinforcing: Saudi Arabia's oblique acknowledgment normalizes UAE's continued deniability; UAE's willingness to accept Israeli cover demonstrates that deniability can be maintained even for operations of significant scale. The Hadi legal vacuum (his death removes the sole formal legal instrument for Saudi Yemen operations) applies additional pressure to this architecture, as Saudi Arabia now also lacks a formal legal basis for Yemen operations for the first time since 2015.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: Both SA domestic_regime and AE domestic_regime carry confidence 3, explicitly capped by the information control architecture (Saudi §III and UAE RSF 164/180 ranking) that prevents open-source confirmation of how the deniability architecture is being received domestically. The analytical claim that the architecture is 'mutually reinforcing' rests on structural inference, not documented coordination.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: The SA and AE deniability approaches are structurally similar but mechanically distinct: Saudi Arabia's channels are wholly domestic (pilgrimage logistics, ceremonial remarks), while UAE's relies on a foreign partner's (Israel's) public statement. These could be independently developed responses to the same structural constraint — the need to acknowledge sacrifice without declaring war — rather than a coordinated deniability doctrine. The MBZ frustration at MBS over military coordination actually suggests the two states are NOT well-coordinated on military matters, which undermines the 'mutually reinforcing' framing.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The structural pressure producing both architectures is identical: both states face domestic audiences who know their sons are fighting and dying, but both states also face Iranian escalation risk from formal declaration. This shared structural constraint independently produces parallel solutions. The MBZ-MBS frustration detail from the AE desk confirms bilateral communication exists, elevating this from coincidence toward coordination — even if the coordination is imperfect.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: The parallel deniability architectures could be entirely independent responses to the same structural constraint, with no meaningful coordination between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi. The absence of Saudi-UAE bilateral diplomatic contact this week, explicitly noted in the AE desk, would support this reading. Each state developed its own institutional vehicle (pilgrimage for Saudi Arabia, partner-cover for UAE) based on its own institutional capabilities rather than a jointly designed doctrine.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Turkey-Proposed Platform as Diplomatic Vehicle for Saudi Arabia's Post-War Institutional Positioning
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: Turkey's Fidan explicitly named Saudi Arabia as a core member of his proposed regional security platform (Turkey-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia-Egypt-Gulf states) in the same week that Saudi Arabia's exclusion from the four multilateral war-termination tracks was analytically documented. The interaction effect is directional: Fidan's platform offer arrives precisely when Saudi Arabia's bilateral diplomatic leverage (real, documented through the MBS-Pezeshkian call and FM Faisal's Gymnich presence) is structurally insufficient to shape the post-war multilateral architecture. Turkey, through its NATO hosting role, pre-existing bilateral access to both Washington and Tehran, and Erdoğan's anticipated Trump bilateral around the June 25 World Cup match, has the institutional access that Saudi Arabia lacks. The proposed platform would give Saudi Arabia a multilateral vehicle where Riyadh is a founding member rather than a late entrant, while giving Turkey a regionally legitimized broker identity that goes beyond the NATO-member framing. Fidan's anti-Israel normalization conditions (explicit 1967-border requirements) are also structurally compatible with Saudi Arabia's public position (Palestinian state as prerequisite), suggesting the two states' public postures are aligned in a way that provides ideological coherence to any joint platform.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: If the platform proposal advances, it would be the most significant new institutional architecture in the region since the Abraham Accords — and notably, one that excludes Israel rather than incorporating it. The Erdoğan-Trump bilateral (if it materializes at the June 25 World Cup match) is the critical near-term test: if Trump endorses or engages with the platform concept, it gains structural viability; if Trump ignores it, it remains a Fidan interview signal without institutional traction.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: The platform proposal is a single interview by a foreign minister whose principal is managing a domestic political crisis (JPMorgan early-election pricing, CHP split). Fidan's proposals may not survive translation into Erdoğan's actual negotiating agenda for the Trump bilateral.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: There is no evidence Saudi Arabia has been consulted on or endorses the platform proposal. The SA desk contains no reference to the Fidan interview or the platform concept. The FM Faisal Gymnich bilateral with Jaishankar is documented; any bilateral with Turkish counterparts in that same format is not mentioned. The proposal may be entirely Turkey's own initiative, with Saudi Arabia as a named beneficiary who has not been asked.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The linkage is structural-consequential rather than evidenced by communication: Fidan named Saudi Arabia specifically in a context where Saudi exclusion from existing multilateral tracks is the documented structural condition. The mechanism — offer of an alternative vehicle to a state that lacks institutional access — is plausible and internally consistent. But without Saudi engagement or response, it remains a unilateral Turkish signal directed at a Saudi need that the Saudi desk independently documents.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: Turkey names Saudi Arabia in the platform primarily for legitimacy-lending purposes — a Saudi Arabia that is fighting an undeclared war and managing Hajj provides Islamic institutional credibility to any Turkey-led security architecture. The invitation is diplomatic branding for the Erdoğan-Trump bilateral rather than a genuine institutional offer to a partner whose exclusion Turkey is trying to remedy.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: India-Saudi Hormuz Convergence: Energy Chokepoint Diplomacy at the EU Gymnich
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: Indian EAM Jaishankar and Saudi FM Faisal bin Farhan held a bilateral at the EU Gymnich informal foreign ministers meeting in Limassol, Cyprus (May 28). The same week, India's 11th Quad FM Meeting in New Delhi produced a joint statement explicitly reaffirming UNCLOS covering the Strait of Hormuz. The connection is directional: India has a documented energy vulnerability to Hormuz closure (RBI Annual Report identifies the West Asia conflict as 'biggest drag on growth in 2026') and has inserted Hormuz UNCLOS language into the Quad's institutional output; Saudi Arabia needs international legitimacy for its combat operations that are — among other objectives — aimed at preventing further Iranian escalation around the same chokepoint. The Gymnich bilateral is the diplomatic contact point between these two structural positions: a country institutionalizing Hormuz navigation rights through the Quad and a country fighting for those navigation rights without being able to say so publicly.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: India is the only country in this region constructing institutional architecture around Hormuz navigation (through the Quad UNCLOS reaffirmation) that does not involve military commitment. Saudi Arabia is the only country in the region with both the fiscal exposure and the direct military engagement on the Hormuz question. The bilateral suggests a complementarity: India provides normative and multilateral cover for the navigation rights principle; Saudi Arabia provides the operational military activity. Whether this converges into a structured partnership or remains a coincident bilateral is the analytical question the Gymnich meeting opens but does not resolve.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: The Jaishankar-Faisal bilateral is documented (Asharq Al-Awsat Tier 2 coverage of the Gymnich meeting notes bilaterals with India, Finland, and Qatar) but the specific content of the India-Saudi bilateral is not reported. The linkage between the bilateral and the Quad Hormuz language is structural inference — both events occurred in the same week but no source documents them as connected.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: The Quad UNCLOS/Hormuz language may have been drafted before the Gymnich bilateral and reflects the standing Quad institutional commitment to freedom of navigation rather than a Saudi-India specific alignment. Jaishankar attended the Gymnich as part of India's active multilateral week (Quad, BRICS Tourism, Shangri-La in the same period) — the Saudi bilateral may be one of many routine ministerial contacts rather than a specifically Hormuz-focused engagement. The SA desk does not connect the Gymnich Jaishankar bilateral to Hormuz in its own analysis.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The mechanism exists — both states have documented Hormuz exposure and documented contact in the same week — but the evidence of connection is circumstantial. The Quad Hormuz language is the stronger anchor: India inserted it institutionally; the Saudi bilateral immediately follows. The structural complementarity is real but the evidence of an actual diplomatic coordination around that complementarity is thin.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: The Jaishankar-Faisal bilateral at Gymnich is primarily about West Asia conflict management from India's perspective — India's $80B+ annual crude imports from the Gulf and the millions of Indian diaspora in Saudi Arabia and UAE create standing bilateral agenda items that have nothing specifically to do with the Hormuz UNCLOS Quad language. The bilateral content may have covered diaspora welfare, bilateral trade, and conflict humanitarian consequences rather than Hormuz governance.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Pakistan's Structural Elevation Across Regional Desks: Gulf Security Provider, Iran Mediator, and Turkey's Proposed Platform Member Simultaneously
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: Pakistan appears on three separate country desks this week in structurally elevated roles that reinforce each other. The SA desk confirms Pakistan deployed a jet squadron and thousands of troops to Saudi Arabia under the SMDA and documents deepened interior security cooperation (200 Federal Constabulary personnel training agreement). The TR desk has Fidan explicitly naming Pakistan as a core member of the proposed regional security platform. The PK posture note confirms Rubio designated Pakistan as Washington's 'primary interlocutor' for Iran-US talks, with Field Marshal Munir conducting two Tehran visits in a single week. These three roles — Gulf security provider, Iran-US mediator, Turkey's platform partner — are not independently developed: Pakistan's SMDA military presence in Saudi Arabia provides the credibility that makes Rubio's mediation designation credible; Pakistan's mediation role provides the diplomatic access that makes Turkey's platform inclusion valuable. The three desks are independently documenting a Pakistan that has moved from regional supplicant to structural lynchpin in the space of a single week.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: Pakistan's elevation is the most consequential regional repositioning of the current cycle that is visible only when the SA, TR, and PK reports are read together. No single desk captures the full picture. The structural question is whether Pakistan's positioning is sustainable: the BLA Eid massacre simultaneously documented on the PK desk, and Drop Site News's publication of Cable I-0678 converting the Khan-removal controversy to documentary record, introduce domestic instability vectors that could rapidly undermine the international positioning. A state that cannot protect its own military personnel on a train on Eid morning is on fragile ground as the region's indispensable mediator.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: Pakistan has no formal desk entry this week — the PK posture note is not a confidence-scored weekly assessment. SA and TR desk references to Pakistan carry their own confidence scores (4 each), but claims about Pakistan's domestic sustainability and the BLA attack's implications for Pakistan's positioning cannot be inherited from SA or TR confidence scores. The confidence is capped at 3 to reflect the absence of a scored PK desk assessment.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: The three roles may be more fragile and less synergistic than they appear. Saudi Arabia's interior security cooperation with Pakistan (200 Federal Constabulary personnel) is operationally minor relative to the SMDA military deployment, and the SA desk notes Saudi Interior Minister 'lauds Pakistan's de-escalation role' — a public diplomatic compliment, not a strategic partnership signal. Turkey's platform proposal including Pakistan may reflect Pakistan's geographic and religious legitimacy for a Turkey-led Islamic security architecture rather than an assessment of Pakistan's actual diplomatic capability. Rubio's 'primary interlocutor' designation, if the Iran deal does not close, becomes a liability rather than an asset.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The three desk references to Pakistan are independently arrived at by country desks tracking different signal categories (SA security and diplomatic, TR diplomatic, PK posture) without cross-referencing each other. The fact that all three converge on Pakistan's elevated role without coordination among the desks makes the pattern more analytically reliable, not less — it is not an artifact of analytical framework but of observed behavior across multiple bilateral relationships simultaneously.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: Pakistan's multiple roles may reflect Washington's deliberate construction of a Pakistan-centric Gulf mediation architecture rather than Pakistan's own strategic agency. If Rubio has designated Pakistan as primary interlocutor, Saudi Arabia's deepened security cooperation, and Turkey's inclusion of Pakistan in the platform proposal are downstream effects of a US strategic decision to elevate Pakistan as a managed proxy for regional stabilization — which would mean Pakistan's positioning is as durable as US commitment to that strategy, no more.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: GCC institutional coordination on oil production and fiscal response to the war
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: The OPEC+ July decision is pending (June 7 meeting), and both Saudi Arabia and UAE have documented fiscal pressures from the conflict. However, the SA desk explicitly notes the bilateral Saudi-UAE track is absent — 'no diplomatic contact below multilateral format confirmed this week' — which is incompatible with a coordination dynamic. Aramco's OSP cuts to Asia and ADNOC's Fujairah capacity doubling are responses to different structural pressures (Saudi Arabia managing demand-side cuts; UAE building supply-side bypass infrastructure) driven by different strategic calculations, not a joint production coordination response. Rejected: absence of bilateral contact is explicitly documented; the economic responses are structurally divergent rather than convergent.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: India-Pakistan back-channel coordination on Iran peace architecture
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: India's Quad FM Meeting explicitly produced UNCLOS/Hormuz language — a legal framework that constrains Iranian behavior around the chokepoint. Pakistan's Munir is simultaneously visiting Tehran twice in one week as Iran's designated interlocutor with Washington. These are structurally incompatible approaches — India is institutionalizing navigation rights against Iran's actions while Pakistan is mediating on Iran's behalf — pursued in parallel without any documented coordination. The India-Pakistan relationship at the government level remains adversarial (both sides recently came out of the Pahalgam incident and Operation Sindoor context per prior weeks' analysis). No source across any of the five country reports documents India-Pakistan contact on the Iran file. Rejected: structural incompatibility of the two states' Iran postures; no contact documented; adversarial bilateral baseline makes coordination implausible.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: Turkey-UAE defense industrial collaboration emerging from Turkey's Japan UAV announcement and UAE's EDGE wartime mobilization
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: Turkey's Fidan announced Turkey-Japan UAV development and production cooperation, and UAE's EDGE Group is confirmed on wartime three-shift production rotations. A regional defense industrial parallel is superficially appealing. However, Turkey-Japan UAV cooperation is geographically and institutionally distinct from UAE's EDGE mobilization — one is an export-oriented diversification away from existing partners, the other is domestic wartime surge production. There is no source across either desk documenting Turkey-UAE defense industrial contact. The single Aramco-Turkey GuzelEnerji stake talks mention in the SA desk is energy sector, not defense industrial. Rejected: the two developments address entirely different structural problems through entirely different mechanisms; no documented contact between Turkish and UAE defense industrial actors.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: Parallel domestic regime stabilization through Islamic ceremonial vehicles: Hajj (Saudi Arabia) and Eid Kılıçdaroğlu contact (Turkey)
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: Both Turkey and Saudi Arabia used Eid al-Adha ceremonially in ways that served domestic regime functions — Saudi Arabia through MBS's Mina Palace reception acknowledging military sacrifice within Hajj framing; Turkey through the Kılıçdaroğlu-AKP Eid contact confirming the co-optation mechanism. While analytically interesting as parallel uses of religious occasion for political purposes, the mechanisms are entirely distinct (one is a state managing wartime acknowledgment; the other is a political co-optation of an opposition party leader), the actors are entirely different (MBS vs. Kılıçdaroğlu/AKP), and the Islamic calendar means Eid al-Adha falls in the same week for all Muslim-majority countries every year. The temporal coincidence is structural to the calendar, not to any shared political strategy. Rejected: coincidence dictated by Islamic calendar; mechanisms are structurally unrelated; no analytical value beyond surface-level similarity.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: Iran peace deal absence as a coordinated regional non-development: multiple desks expected closure and none materialized
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: The Iran peace deal non-closure this week is significant (Ghalibaf: 'enemy promise can't be trusted'; Araghchi dismissed reports) but it is a single Iranian decision, not a multi-country regional dynamic. The AE desk correctly flags the non-finalization as a 'meaningful absence'; the TR desk has Fidan claiming the deal is 'closer than ever'; the IN desk notes the seventh consecutive non-confirmation window. These are not parallel country behaviors that require synthesis — they are five country desks independently observing the same Iranian non-action. This belongs in the gaps section, not cross-cutting dynamics. Rejected: the dynamic is Iranian non-action observed by multiple states, not a cross-country pattern among the five analyzed states.

gaps.expected_dynamic: Iran peace deal closure generating downstream regional repositioning across Gulf states and South Asian mediators
gaps.observed: Iran peace deal explicitly non-finalized: Ghalibaf stated 'enemy promise can't be trusted'; Araghchi dismissed deal reports as speculation by May 31. This is the seventh consecutive non-confirmation window for India's desk. Multiple desks (AE, TR, PK posture) framed the week against imminent deal closure that did not occur.
gaps.assessment: The non-closure is analytically significant across the region because each country's posture calculus has been partially suspended pending deal resolution. Saudi Arabia's fiscal paradox sharpens with every week of war continuation. UAE's deniability architecture becomes more exposed with each additional week of documented offensive operations. Pakistan's Munir mediation visits to Tehran have no confirmed output. Turkey's Fidan 'closer than ever' claim is contradicted by Iranian public statements. The gap between the deal's perceived imminence (as of May 24) and its actual non-materialization suggests either a deliberate Iranian delay strategy or that the 'largely negotiated' framing was premature. The regional significance is that every country in this analysis has organized some portion of its posture around an imminent deal that is not arriving.

gaps.expected_dynamic: Saudi Arabia-UAE bilateral coordination on military operations and post-war political architecture given their joint offensive participation
gaps.observed: The AE desk explicitly documents Saudi criticism of UAE's military approach (Saudi Arabia warning UAE's strikes raised retaliation risk across the region) and MBZ's frustration at MBS when Gulf neighbors refused to coordinate military responses. The SA desk records no Saudi-UAE bilateral diplomatic contact this week. The two states are operating the region's most active offensive military operations against Iran without a documented coordination architecture.
